title: Prospect Park — Lenape Ridge and Road
summary: Prospect Park lies in Lenapehoking. Lenape families planted the Flatbush lands beside an ancient road that is now Flatbush Avenue. Colonial seizure, war and removal followed, but Native Brooklyn continues, from Lefferts Historic House to neighborhoods across the borough.
address_label: Prospect Park Boathouse, 101 East Drive, on the Lullwater, Brooklyn, NY

why_this_matters: Prospect Park looks like countryside, but its ridge, road and planting lands are Lenape places. A walk from Battle Pass to Lefferts Historic House follows that history from Lenape fields to colonial seizure, war and Lenape return.
introduction_content:
Prospect Park’s ridge, woods and wetlands belong to Lenapehoking, the homeland of the Lenape. The Historic House Trust describes the Flatbush lands beside the park as a hub of commerce and culture for thousands of years before Europeans arrived. Lenape families grew corn, beans and squash here, and Flatbush Avenue follows an ancient Lenape road.[1]

Brooklyn’s first people probably used no single name for themselves beyond Lenape, “People.” They named themselves by home place: someone living at Nayack, today’s Fort Hamilton, was a Nayack; at Marechkawieck, now Brooklyn Heights, a Marechkawieck; at Canarsie, a Canarsie.[2]
history_content:
A ridge shaped by ice

The park’s hills belong to a rocky ridge that runs from Green-Wood Cemetery through Prospect Park to Mount Prospect Park; only four passes cut through it.[3] When the last glacier melted, buried blocks of ice left hollows called kettles. Many filled with water and became wetlands, and some of the park’s wetlands come from those older natural forces.[4]

A 1652 deed for New Utrecht describes land running from Gowanus “across the hills” to Mechawanienck, a name William Wallace Tooker read as an “old Indian trail or path.”[5] If Tooker is right, Lenape paths crossed these hills long before the park. Read more at Mechawanienck.

Fields taken, families displaced

The Historic House Trust writes that settlers under the Dutch West India Company took the Flatbush lands by force in 1645. That fighting and later conflicts pushed many Lenape east onto Long Island and west into New Jersey and Pennsylvania. In the 1660s the Lefferts family received 100 acres of land taken from the Lenape.[1]

In 1679 the traveler Jasper Danckaerts found Najack families at today’s Fort Hamilton living in a bark longhouse beside their maize fields. Jacques Cortelyou had bought their land; he let them keep a small corner, and they paid him twenty bushels of maize a year for it.[6] The last tract of Native land in Brooklyn was sold in 1684. Many families moved east to Rockaway, Massapequa and Hempstead; others followed the Nayack sachem Mattano to Staten Island and New Jersey, or went north to the Hudson and Delaware valleys.[2]

Battle Pass, 1776

Flatbush Pass, where East Drive now climbs between the hills, was marked by a large tree called the Dongan Oak, which was chopped down to slow the British advance. On August 27, 1776, Hessian troops pushed up the pass while British forces came from behind, and the Americans fled across today’s Long Meadow. The memory of Battle Pass was part of the reason this site was chosen for Prospect Park in the 1850s.[3]

A park built on Lenape ground

Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux later reshaped this topography to create Prospect Park.[3] The Boathouse on the Lullwater was built in 1905.[7] In 1918 the Lefferts farmhouse was moved into the park from the corner of Flatbush Avenue and Maple Street.[1]

Native Brooklyn continues

Displacement carried Lenape families as far as Oklahoma, Wisconsin and Canada. The Historic House Trust notes that some Lenape stayed and others are returning to their ancestral land.[1] Today Lefferts Historic House invites visitors to explore stories of resistance and resilience by the Indigenous people of Lenapehoking, together with the stories of Africans enslaved by the Lefferts family.[8]

Brooklyn has also been home to Native people from other nations. From the 1920s, Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake and their families built a community in Boerum Hill, known as Little Caughnawaga.[9] In 1986, Robert Grumet described Brooklyn’s Native community as the largest in the greater New York area.[2]
whereintheworld_content:
The green dot marks the Boathouse at 101 East Drive, on the Lullwater.[7] Walk north on East Drive to find three bronze plaques for Battle Pass and the site of the Dongan Oak.[3] Lefferts Historic House stands at the park’s eastern edge beside Flatbush Avenue.[10] Stay on park paths and help care for the woods and water.

Continue to Brooklyn’s colonial land claims, Gowanus or Nayack.
